query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A data‐driven surrogate model that incorporates microstructural variables (e.g., grain size, defect density) and the effects of 1 wt.% oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr can provide conductivity predictions across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K that are significantly more accurate than conventional analytical models assuming perfect crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and realistic microstructural features (defects, grain size distributions) generated during standard processing.
generation.intervention: Train a machine learning surrogate model on experimental thermophysical data (specifically conductivity) from the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes, including microstructural descriptors and oxygen content as explicit inputs.
generation.conditions: The model applies to bulk specimens of HfNbTaTiZr containing ~1 wt.% oxygen; predictive accuracy is evaluated over cryogenic (0–200 K) and elevated (300–1200 K) temperature regimes with a blind hold-out test set in the intermediate 200–300 K range.
generation.structural_mediator: The inclusion of measurable microstructural variables, such as grain size and defect density, mediates the influence of interstitial oxygen and defect scattering on electronic/phonon conduction pathways.
generation.mechanism: By modeling the effects of defects and oxygen-induced scattering directly, the surrogate approach overcomes the limitations of idealized, defect-free analytical predictions. The ML model learns the empirical relationships between microstructure, composition, and temperature-dependent conduction phenomena, leading to improved accuracy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The surrogate model will predict electrical or thermal conductivity within a 15% error margin compared to experimental hold-out data in the 200–300 K range, outperforming conventional analytical models that neglect microstructural imperfections.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical predictions, which are based on perfect-crystal assumptions and neglect defect and oxygen scattering effects, typically show larger discrepancies when applied to real, defect-bearing materials.
generation.boundary: The model is valid for bulk HfNbTaTiZr with 1 wt.% oxygen over the specified temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K). Its accuracy outside these conditions or for substantially different oxygen levels/microstructures is untested.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement will depend on the quality and comprehensiveness of the training dataset and microstructural characterizations. The predicted <15% error margin is an estimate that may vary with data limitations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen and measure conductivity in the intermediate temperature range (200–300 K). Independently train the surrogate model on conductivity data exclusively recorded in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes, withholding the 200–300 K data. After training, compare the ML model predictions to the experimental measurements in the 200–300 K interval.
measurements: Temperature-dependent conductivity measurements (electrical or thermal) between 200 K and 300 K.
Microstructural characterization (grain size, defect density) of the samples.
Oxygen content verification by chemical analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the absolute percentage error between the surrogate model predictions and the experimental conductivity measurements in the 200–300 K range exceeds 15%, the hypothesis that the ML approach offers a significant accuracy improvement over analytical models will be falsified.

These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Only one prior study in this collection (PMC11077685) focuses on precisely the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy. That work addresses additive manufacturing routes and oxidation-resistant coatings, illustrating the stability and mechanical strength benefits of minor interstitial additions (notably oxygen) even at elevated temperatures. However, it does not explore detailed conduction properties—particularly in the cryogenic (0–200 K) range—and does not provide predictive frameworks that account explicitly for the scattering effects of 1 wt.% oxygen or other real-world defects. Thus, while the alloy’s high-temperature performance is established, the effect of oxygen on transport properties across a broad temperature range remains insufficiently quantified, leaving an open gap in accurately predicting thermal or electrical conductivity under realistic (i.e., non-ideal, oxygen-bearing) conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite the recognized need, no published work in this subset has yet offered a reliable, quantitative method to predict conduction in HfNbTaTiZr from near-zero to elevated temperatures when 1 wt.% oxygen and defect structures are present. Existing analytical models, which assume perfect single crystals, fail to capture the scattering and phonon/electron transport complexities induced by real-world compositions and morphologies.
decision.lever: Train a surrogate model on measured HfNbTaTiZr thermophysical data that explicitly includes microstructural variables (grain size, defect density) and oxygen concentration (≈1 wt.%). Calibrate and validate the model on published 0–200 K and 300–1200 K experimental conductivity data, then hold out a further set of conductivity measurements at an intermediate range (≈200–300 K) for final blind comparison to test predictive accuracy.
decision.why: By capturing composition, microstructure, and temperature as direct inputs, a ML-based method addresses defect scattering, interstitial oxygen effects, and high-temperature complexity—factors that existing perfect-crystal analytical models neglect. The approach is supported by prior demonstrations (PMC11077685) that highlight oxygen’s significant effect on mechanical and thermal behavior in HfNbTaTiZr. If the model’s predictions deviate from the withheld conductivity data by more than, e.g., 15%, the hypothesis that data-driven approaches can outperform purely analytical models in real, defect-bearing material regimes would be falsified.
